title: US Drone Startup Powerus Inks Pakistan Army Deal as Drone Exports Reshape South Asia; India Opens Stealth Frigate Race to Competitive Bidding
subhead: A Florida counter-drone firm tied to the Trump orbit signed an MOU and initial order with the Pakistan Army on Sept 16, while India shifted its Project 17B stealth frigate programme from nomination to competitive bidding — two moves that signal how drone commerce and procurement competition are reshaping South Asian defense ties.

sections.heading: Powerus-Pakistan: A Trump-Orbit Drone Startup Enters the Pakistan Market
sections.body:
Florida-based drone maker Powerus signed a memorandum of understanding with the Pakistan Army on Sept 16 that includes an initial drone-related order, co-founder Brett Velicovich told Reuters. The deal follows a Powerus delegation meeting Pakistan's Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir at GHQ in Rawalpindi, per the Quetta Voice report. The initial order involves power systems, with technical details withheld for security reasons, according to devdiscourse.

The company — which sells aerial and maritime drones for military and industrial use and has been described by the New York Times as a Florida startup building low-cost counterdrone systems amid the Iran conflict — is due to merge with Aureus Greenway Holdings, a publicly traded company backed by two of Donald Trump's sons, as Times of Israel reported. The deal dovetails with the improving Washington-Islamabad relationship under the current administration, which has been advancing mutual economic and defense initiatives.
sections.whyItMatters: A US private drone vendor with presidential-family ties establishing a direct channel to the Pakistan Army marks a notable commercial opening of the Pakistan market to American unmanned systems — terrain long dominated by Chinese suppliers — and adds a commercial layer to the broader US-Pakistan rapprochement.

sections.heading: India Opens Project 17B Stealth Frigates to Competitive Bidding
sections.body:
The Indian Navy has issued a request for proposal for seven advanced stealth frigates under Project 17B, worth an estimated Rs 70,000 crore (~$8.4 billion), this time through competitive bidding rather than the nomination route, the Times of India reported. Earlier programmes (Project 15A, 15B, and 17A) were awarded directly to defence PSUs without competition. Category A shipyards — Mazagon Dock, Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers, Goa Shipyard, and Cochin Shipyard — are the likely recipients of the RFP.

Dubbed Next Generation Frigates, the P17B vessels are a follow-on to the Nilgiri-class (Project 17A) and will feature enhanced low-observable stealth, advanced sensors and vertical launch systems. Expected weaponry includes BrahMos cruise missiles, indigenous electronic warfare suites and advanced air-defense missiles, per the Times of India.
sections.whyItMatters: Shifting a major warship programme from nomination to cost-and-capability competition signals a quiet procurement reform inside Indian naval acquisition, potentially driving down cost and pressuring public shipyards to compete on performance — even as India keeps the entire programme domestic.

sections.heading: Ukraine War Pushes Europe Toward Bigger, Cheaper Missile Arsenals
sections.body:
European militaries are increasingly exploring cheaper missiles and interceptors after conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East exposed the limits of small, high-end inventories, Reuters reported. Russia's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine demonstrated that modern warfare depletes weapon supplies faster than peacetime planning assumed. Douglas Barrie of the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) has flagged the risk of relying solely on high-end weapons, per a devdiscourse summary of the same reporting.

The shift spans established players and startups — Lockheed Martin and MBDA are among firms weighing scalable production of low-cost systems alongside startups, as European defense industry reorients toward large-scale manufacturing over boutique high-end lines.
sections.whyItMatters: The affordability-vs-lethality tradeoff is now the defining debate in European missile demand. Cheap, mass-producible interceptors and strike weapons are becoming the priority over premium systems — a demand signal that will shape which missile lines European industry scales up for years.

sections.heading: Hanwha and Lockheed UK Pitch Counter-Drone Armoured Turret at DVD 2026
sections.body:
Hanwha Aerospace and Lockheed Martin UK unveiled a new 40 mm counter-drone configuration of the AS21 Redback infantry fighting vehicle at Defense Vehicle Dynamics in Millbrook on Sept 16, Army Recognition reported. The turret pairs CTA International's 40 mm cased-telescoped cannon with Lockheed Martin UK's SkyKeeper counter-UAS command-and-control system, integrated using Generic Vehicle Architecture at Lockheed's Bedfordshire facility.

The design contrasts with the Australian Army's LAND 400 Phase 3 Redback, which uses a two-person Elbit MT30 Mk 2-derived turret with a 30 mm Bushmaster II cannon and Spike LR2 anti-tank missiles. The new configuration shifts emphasis from anti-armour reach toward networked counter-drone operations, letting an IFV contribute to a wider recognized air picture. Live demonstrations are planned for 2027 in Canada and South Korea, per Army Recognition.
sections.whyItMatters: The Redback variant points to how NATO armour is evolving in response to drone-saturated combat in Ukraine: distributing counter-UAS capability across the armoured formation rather than concentrating it in dedicated air-defense vehicles — and giving Hanwha an adaptable export configuration beyond the Australian baseline.

sections.heading: Germany Moves Toward Fourth Type 424 SIGINT Ship as Programme Runs Ahead of Schedule
sections.body:
Germany is advancing plans for a fourth Type 424 fleet intelligence vessel, with Defence Minister Boris Pistorius saying the new capability profile calls for four ships and sending the proposal to parliament, defence-industry.eu reported. The announcement came as Rheinmetall laid the keel of the third ship at its Peene-Werft yard in Wolgast several months ahead of schedule, with the second vessel under parallel construction.

The ~130-metre SIGINT ships, equipped with advanced sensor technology for monitoring the electromagnetic spectrum across land, sea and air, are due to enter service gradually from 2029, according to Pistorius. The navy will work with the Cyber and Information Domain Service on intelligence gathering. Vessels are to be towed to Rheinmetall's Blohm+Voss yard in Hamburg for final outfitting. Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger called the ahead-of-schedule keel laying a testament to the shipyard's capabilities.
sections.whyItMatters: Expanding the SIGINT fleet to four ships reflects Germany's post-Ukraine investment in maritime intelligence and surveillance across the Baltic and North Atlantic — and hands Rheinmetall a multi-ship naval backlog well beyond its traditional land-systems base.

sections.heading: US Army Commits Nearly $5 Billion to Laser Missile Defense for Its Helicopter Fleet
sections.body:
The US Army awarded Northrop Grumman $4.8 billion to produce laser-based Common Infrared Countermeasures (CIRCM) systems, Task & Purpose reported, citing the contract notice of Sept 8. The systems protect helicopters from shoulder-fired Stinger-class missiles by tracking incoming munitions and jamming their seekers.

According to Northrop Grumman, CIRCM is installed on over 550 Army Apache, Chinook and Black Hawk helicopters, with plans to equip all Army rotary-wing aircraft, including the future MV-75. The new laser weighs about 50 pounds versus roughly 160 pounds for the older ATIRCM system it replaces, per Northrop data cited by Task & Purpose. The contract runs through 2035 and also supports foreign military sales of the technology. Air Force interest is in early review, an Army spokesperson said.
sections.whyItMatters: A near-$5 billion commitment to unlimited-magazine laser countermeasures reflects a broader US pivot away from expendable flares toward directed-energy self-protection, and signals that missile-threat evolution — not just drones — is driving survivability spending across rotary-wing fleets.

bottomLine: Sept 16-17 brought no single decisive event, but a cluster of procurement signals: a Trump-orbiting US drone startup opened a direct channel to the Pakistan Army; India thrust its flagship stealth frigate programme into open competition domestically; Europe's missile demand shifted emphatically toward cheaper, mass-producible arsenals; and both German naval SIGINT and US helicopter laser self-protection spending confirmed the post-Ukraine rearmament is broad-based. The through-line is industrial: from Pakistan to India to NATO, the driver is who can scale affordable production and adapt quickly — drones on one end, directed energy on the other — rather than who fields the single most exotic platform.
sources: Reuters, Times of India, devdiscourse, Quetta Voice, Times of Israel, New York Times, Army Recognition, defence-industry.eu, Task & Purpose, Intelligence Online
